details:
**Battle of Lützen (1632)**
A Swedish victory over Albrecht von Wallenstein's imperial army, fought in heavy fog, in which the Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus was killed. It is the most common battle clue for the war, and the fog was so famous that "Lützen fog" came to describe a particularly thick fog.

**Second Defenestration of Prague (1618)**
The event that started the war. Bohemian Protestant nobles threw two Catholic imperial regents (and their secretary) out of a window of Prague Castle. All three survived, which Catholics credited to angels and Protestants to a pile of manure they landed in.

**Peace of Westphalia (1648)**
The set of treaties negotiated at Münster and Osnabrück that ended the war. It reaffirmed and expanded the Peace of Augsburg's principle that rulers chose their state's religion, adding Calvinism, and it is often seen as the origin of the modern system of sovereign states.

**Battle of White Mountain (1620)**
The decisive battle of the war's Bohemian phase. Catholic League forces under Count Tilly crushed the Bohemian Protestants who had elected Frederick V of the Palatinate as their king, and 27 rebel leaders were later executed in Prague's Old Town Square.

**Gustavus Adolphus**
The Swedish king, nicknamed the "Lion of the North," who entered the war in 1630 on the Protestant side. He used shallower, more mobile linear formations and light field artillery, won at Breitenfeld and the Lech (Rain), and died at Lützen; his daughter Christina succeeded him.

**Frederick V, the "Winter King"**
The Elector Palatine who accepted the Bohemian crown in 1619 and lost it after a single winter when he was defeated at White Mountain. He fled into exile in the Dutch Republic, and parts of his library, the Bibliotheca Palatina, were given to Pope Gregory XV.

**Count of Tilly and the Sack of Magdeburg**
Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly, commanded the Catholic League army, winning at White Mountain and at Lutter (1626) against Christian IV of Denmark. His forces sacked and burned Protestant Magdeburg in 1631, killing most of its inhabitants, and the destruction gave rise to the term "Magdeburgization." He was mortally wounded at the Battle of Rain on the Lech River in 1632.

**Battle of Breitenfeld (1631)**
Gustavus Adolphus's first great victory, in which his Swedish and Saxon army routed Tilly's imperial forces near Leipzig. It established Sweden as the leading Protestant power in the war.

**Albrecht von Wallenstein**
The Bohemian nobleman who raised huge armies for Emperor Ferdinand II, paying for them by making conquered lands support them ("war feeds itself," bellum se ipsum alet). He failed at the Siege of Stralsund (1628) and fought Gustavus at Lützen. Suspected of treason, he was assassinated at Eger (Cheb) in 1634 by officers including Walter Leslie, and he is the subject of Friedrich Schiller's Wallenstein trilogy, which includes The Piccolominis.

**Four phases: Bohemian, Danish, Swedish, French**
The traditional way of dividing the war. Each phase is named for the main party fighting the Habsburgs at the time, ending with French intervention under Cardinal Richelieu and later Cardinal Mazarin.

**Christian IV and the Treaty of Lübeck (1629)**
Christian IV of Denmark entered the war in 1625, a phase sometimes called the Low Saxon War, but was beaten by Tilly at Lutter and by Wallenstein. The Treaty of Lübeck ended Danish involvement.

**Battle of Rocroi (1643)**
A French victory under the young Duc d'Enghien, later known as the Grand Condé, over the Spanish army of Francisco de Melo. It was the first major defeat of the famous Spanish tercio infantry formations and signaled the decline of Spanish military power.

**War of the Mantuan Succession**
A side conflict (1628–1631) that broke out when the main Gonzaga line of the Duchy of Mantua died out with Vincenzo II. France and the Habsburgs fought over the succession, which threatened Spain's "Spanish Road" for moving troops to the Netherlands.

**Battle of Nördlingen (1634)**
A major Catholic victory in which imperial and Spanish forces under the future Ferdinand III and the Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand destroyed the main Swedish army. It led the German Protestant princes to make peace and prompted France to enter the war directly.

**Hakkapeliitta**
The Finnish light cavalry who served in Gustavus Adolphus's Swedish army, famous for their charges and their war cry "hakkaa päälle" ("cut them down").

**Witch trials of Würzburg and Bamberg**
Some of the largest witch hunts in European history took place during the war. Prince-Bishop Philipp Adolf von Ehrenberg led the trials in Würzburg, and Prince-Bishop Johann Georg Fuchs von Dornheim built the Drudenhaus prison for accused witches in Bamberg.
